newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU policy on airline aid back in the news.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU policy on airline aid back in the news.

text.p: European Commission efforts to police state-funded airline bail-outs are set to return to the headlines in the coming months as decisions fall due on rescue plans for Italy's Alitalia, Air France and others.

At stake for Alitalia is a request for Commission clearance, with as few conditions as possible, for a package of cash payments, share sales and pension subsidies worth nearly 3.5 trillion lire ($2.1 billion)in the run-up to 2000.

Air France, meanwhile, will be looking to the European Court of First Instance in Luxembourg for a ruling on the legality of the Commission's approval in 1994 of its 20 billion French franc ($3.5 billion) rescue package.

Other state-owned airlines under Commission scrutiny include Olympic Airways, which is in the dock along with the Greek government for alleged breaches in conditions linked to its 54 billion drachma ($206.9 million) plan of 1994.
The Commission is also checking on Iberia to see that it sells assets as required in last year's decision to approve the airline's 87 billion peseta ($617.5 million) aid package.

All these cases, along with earlier ones involving Ireland's Aer Lingus, Belgium's Sabena and TAP Air Portugal, have prompted angry condemnation from private-sector competitors, who accuse the Commission of singing the song of air liberalisation while nodding through billions of dollars in unfair assistance.

Gerrit Schohe, a lawyer with the firm Feddersen Laule, Scherzberg & Ohle Hansen Ewerwahn, says Commission scrutiny of aid requests takes place in undue secrecy following ill-defined rules which create legal uncertainty for competitors.

"The current procedure for state aid is unfair, undemocratic and unacceptable in the highly competitive transport sector," Schohe told a Forum Europe conference on state aid in the EU's transport sector.
"No company can afford to rest easy while state aid authorisation remains behind closed doors in the hands of an institution which has the power to change or distort a market overnight," he said.
Schohe criticised the Commission's use of the "private investor principle" to judge whether planned payments, and associated restructuring plans, would pass muster on the financial markets.
"The flaw in this principle is that no one can determine what a 'typical investor' would do when considering, for example, whether to inject capital into an ailing airline."
COMMISSION REJECTS CRITICISM OF ITS CRITERIA
Philip Lowe, chief aide to European Commissioner Neil Kinnock, said the Commission was aware of problems related to state-aid decisions but rejected criticisms of its criteria.

"Everyone knows that the Commission cannot distinguish between a publicly owned and a privately owned company, it's not allowed to. Where only public investors are involved then we have to rely on this principle," Lowe told the same conference.

"I think we have to recognise that the Commission is in the end taking a difficult decision and putting that decision to (EU member states) may not help improve the independence of that decision," he added.
Lowe said state-owned airlines needed some way to raise fresh capital, which inevitably attracted state-aid inquiries.

While academic talk on what a theoretical investor might pay is one thing, uncertainties in EU law are such that aid decisions are inevitably influenced by the political realities in national capitals, where governments tinker with sacred flag carriers at their peril, risking protest strikes.
Germany's part-privatised airline Lufthansa AG, half-way between public and private ownership, is in a better position than most to be non-partisan.
Thomas Kropp, the company's government affairs specialist, said the issue for his company was how airlines spent their aid.

"My company is totally not against state aid as such because we understand if a company has to restructure itself. What we cannot understand is if this huge amount of money is misused and I think this is a big problem," Kropp told the conference.
"This is the task for the Commission in future cases, this aid has to be used only for restructuring, not at all for price wars."
CHALLENGE TO AIR FRANCE AID DECISION

Six airlines led by British Airways, Scandinavian Airlines System and the Dutch airline, KLM, have challenged the Commission's decision to grant the Air France aid before the European Court of First Instance.

Romano Subiotto of Cleary, Gottlieb, Steen & Hamilton, representing the airlines bringing the case, told Reuters their main complaints were that the Commission had based its decision on an Air France recovery plan carrying little detail, that the amount granted was over-generous and that attached conditions were vague and unenforceable.

He said that if the court annulled the decision, the Commission would have to reassess its analysis and perhaps impose stricter conditions on the French carrier or oblige it to repay some of the aid money to the French government.
Alain Weill, Air France's head of European and industry affairs, refused to comment in detail ahead of the case, telling Reuters by telephone that he had full confidence in the Commission decision.

Herman De Croo, the Belgian liberal politician who oversaw a Commission-sponsored report on aviation in 1994, said that despite EU court action by airlines, progress in stamping out unfair aid had been far slower than he had expected.

"Community people are so obsessed by the single European currency question that anything that could spoil collaboration with member states is eliminated," he said, characterising Commission efforts as worth a "B minus" on a scale of A to C.
